# Yogurt and human health across history, culture, and science: Lessons for modern aging populations

**Authors:** Sarah Jaehwa Park; Howard D Sesso; Ariela R Orkaby; Kerry L Ivey

**Affiliations:** aOsher Center for Integrative Health, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | bDivision of Preventive Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | cDepartment of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | dNew England Geriatric Research, Education, and Clinical Center, VA Boston Healthcare System, Boston, MA, United States | eDivision of Aging, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | fDepartment of Medicine, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States

## Abstract

Yogurt is an ancient fermented milk product obtained through the action of specific lactic acid bacteria. It gained widespread modern popularity in the early 1900s when it was proposed as the secret to extending lifespan. In the 1950s, however, dairy fats became highly controversial due to its high saturated fat content, which formed the basis of the “diet-heart hypothesis.” In recent decades, there has been a global resurgence of scientific and public interest in yogurt due to growing awareness of its distinct health benefits which are largely ascribed to its provision of probiotics and bioactive compounds. As such, yogurt products have been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach to modulate the production of gut microbiota-derived metabolites implicated in the development and progression of aging-related chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. However, numerous questions remain regarding its therapeutic potential and underlying biological mechanisms. In this review, we examine current evidence within historical and cultural contexts to help refine research hypotheses and inform public health strategies to support healthy aging, with a particular focus on cardiometabolic health.

Keywords: Dairy, Fermented milk, Yogurt, Functional foods, Cardiovascular disease, Aging, Gut microbiota, Lactobacillus bifidobacterium

## Introduction

Yogurt is a semisolid fermented milk product with origins tracing back several millennia. It first entered scientific discourse in the early 20th century when Élie Metchnikoff proposed that lactic acid bacteria in yogurt could suppress putrefactive intestinal microbes he believed accelerated aging and thereby prolong life [1]. Although his mechanistic understanding was limited by the science of his time, his central insight that diet, gut microbiota, and human health are interconnected has proven remarkably prescient. More than a century later, gut dysbiosis has been implicated in a broad spectrum of age-related diseases [[1], [2], [3]], and yogurt has reemerged as a promising dietary strategy to restore the microbial diversity and balance that often decline with aging. Indeed, yogurt consumption has been associated with a distinct gut microbiome characteristic of healthy aging [4,5] and lower risks of cardiometabolic disease, dementia, osteoporosis, colorectal cancer, and even mortality [[6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]], raising the possibility that it could meaningfully contribute to longevity.

Despite strong epidemiological evidence, the long-term effects of yogurt interventions on clinical age-related health outcomes remain largely unexplored in humans, and the biological mechanisms underlying these associations are not yet fully understood. Accordingly, we explored yogurt’s evolution from an ancient fermented milk product to a modern functional food to provide context for its potential health benefits, refine research hypotheses, and inform contemporary strategies for healthy aging, with a particular focus on cardiometabolic health.

## Current state of knowledge: Yogurt overcomes the dairy fat paradox

Dairy foods are rich sources of essential nutrients that support healthy aging, including high-quality protein, B vitamins, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus [12]. These nutrients contribute to the preservation of cognitive function, bone health, and skeletal muscle mass in older adults, potentially reducing the risk of osteoporosis, sarcopenia, and age-related functional decline [[13], [14], [15]]. Despite these benefits, the health impacts of full-fat dairy products have long been debated because of their high saturated fat content and potential implications for cardiometabolic disease, a major contributor to unhealthy aging. Decades of guidance favoring low-fat and fat-free dairy have been shaped by concerns that saturated fat may increase serum cholesterol and thereby the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and that its higher caloric density might promote weight gain [16]. The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans mark a notable departure from this position, now encouraging consumption of full-fat dairy [17]. This shift reflects an evolving evidence base linking full-fat dairy products to neutral and, in some cases, reduced risk of cardiometabolic disease [9,[18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]]—a phenomenon known as the dairy fat paradox (Fig. 1).

*Fig. 1: Timeline of key historical, cultural, and scientific events that shaped the evolution of yogurt from an ancient fermented milk product to a modern functional food.*

The updated Guidelines have nonetheless drawn criticism from scientists who note that the promotion of full-fat dairy and animal protein sources is inconsistent with the concurrent recommendation to limit saturated fat intake to <10% of total calories, and have raised concerns regarding potential influence from the dairy and meat industries in their development [26,27]. Moreover, the Guidelines do not consider the dairy type or matrix, despite growing evidence that fermented dairy products may confer distinct health benefits beyond nutrient provision through their live cultures and bioactive compounds [28,29]. Yogurt, in particular, is the most extensively studied fermented dairy product in relation to healthy aging and favorable cardiometabolic outcomes, and is therefore the primary focus of this review.

Meta-analyses and cohort studies consistently show that yogurt consumption—regardless of fat content—is associated with lower risks of CVD [10,30], type 2 diabetes (T2D) [18,19,[31], [32], [33]], obesity [18], and metabolic syndrome (MetS) [34]. These associations are generally stronger than those observed for other dairy foods, such as milk or cheese, which are often neutral or modestly protective [35]. Although cheese is also fermented, yogurt’s superior cardiometabolic profile is likely due to its higher levels of probiotics and bioactive compounds, lower sodium and caloric content, and association with healthier dietary patterns [[36], [37], [38]]. Collectively, these characteristics position yogurt as a unique example of how the dairy matrix and fermentation process may mitigate the potential adverse cardiometabolic effects traditionally attributed to saturated fat while supporting healthy aging.

## Methods

This narrative review synthesized evidence on the historical, cultural, and scientific significance of yogurt in relation to aging and major age-related diseases. Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and JSTOR, using combinations and variations of the following key words: "fermented milk,” “yogurt,” “dairy,” “probiotics,” “lactase persistence,” “gut microbiome,” “cardiovascular disease,” “diabetes,” “obesity,” “metabolic syndrome,” “aging,” “health,” “wellness,” “history of dairy,” and “nutrition history.” We included peer-reviewed articles, historical texts, periodicals, and government or organizational guidelines published from antiquity to the present. Bibliographies of relevant articles were also manually reviewed to identify additional sources.

To synthesize evidence across disciplines, this review was structured thematically, following yogurt’s path from its ancient origins to modern scientific inquiry. While this review primarily focuses on yogurt, we also considered the broader historical context of fermented dairy products because yogurt did not emerge in isolation, but rather as part of a wider evolutionary and cultural transition toward fermented milk consumption. However, synthesis and interpretation of scientific evidence was primarily restricted to yogurt-related research, and other fermented dairy products are discussed only where necessary to provide important historical context.

## Origins and history of yogurt

### Ancient milk and the emergence of fermented dairy products

During the Neolithic period, milk represented a novel and nutritionally valuable resource, providing protein, fats, carbohydrates, essential vitamins and minerals, and water. Chemical evidence of milk fat residues preserved in Neolithic pottery suggests that dairying began in northwestern Anatolia as early as the 7th millennium B.C. [39], before spreading into other parts of Europe and Africa between the 6th and 4th millennia B.C. [[40], [41], [42], [43], [44], [45]]. However, milk consumption in early human populations would have been limited by the widespread absence of lactase persistence [46], as well as by its vulnerability to rapid spoilage and pathogenic contamination [47]. Thus, it is widely hypothesized that fermented dairy products such as yogurt and cheese emerged as a cultural adaptation to preserve milk and reduce its lactose content.

While early cheese-making is inferred from perforated ceramic vessels resembling modern strainers used to separate curds from whey [48], the origins of yogurt remain elusive, as its production neither requires specialized equipment nor leaves distinctive chemical traces. Nevertheless, historians postulate that yogurt was first discovered inadvertently in the Near East or Central Asia around 5000 BCE, when nomadic herders carried milk in pouches made from animal intestines, allowing native microbes to initiate spontaneous fermentation [49]. Evidence supporting this practice comes from traditional pastoral societies that use similar methods to make fermented milk products such as kumis and garris [50,51].

The biochemical processes underlying industrial milk fermentation provide further support for this hypothesis. Lactose, the primary carbohydrate in milk, is a disaccharide composed of glucose and galactose linked by a β-1,4-glycosidic bond [52]. During fermentation, lactic acid bacteria produce β-galactosidases that effectively substitute for lactase by cleaving lactose into its two more absorbable constituent monosaccharides [52]. This substantially reduces the lactose content in milk, making it more digestible, although trace amounts remain in the final product. The liberated monosaccharides are then fermented into lactic acid, lowering the pH of milk and inhibiting the growth of food spoilage microorganisms at ambient temperatures [47,53]. Certain strains further this biopreservative effect by producing additional antimicrobial compounds, such as hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins, which can suppress foodborne pathogens like Listeria monocytogenes and Clostridium botulinum [54]. Through these mechanisms, fermentation not only improves the digestibility of milk but also enhances its shelf life and safety. In doing so, it likely helped facilitate broader adoption of dairying while providing meaningful survival advantages by extending the nutritional value of milk beyond infancy.

### The gene-culture coevolution and host adaptations

Over generations, continued exposure to residual lactose in fermented milk likely allowed individuals to tolerate fresh milk in limited quantities or intermittently. Direct evidence of milk intake, identified through the detection of whey protein preserved in ancient dental calculus, appears between the 5th and 3rd millennia B.C., long before lactase persistence alleles became more prevalent [45,[55], [56], [57], [58], [59]]. Selective pressure for lactase persistence would have intensified during periods of drought or famine, when humans could rely on fresh milk as a source of hydration while extracting additional calories from lactose digestion [46]. Today, lactase persistence remains prevalent in approximately one-third of the global population, particularly among individuals of northern European ancestry and, to a lesser extent, some African, Middle Eastern, and South Asian lineages [52].

Emerging hypotheses also suggest that selection for lactase persistence may have extended beyond lactose digestion alone, favoring genetic variants involved in lipid metabolism. This possibility is illustrated by the Maasai pastoralists of East Africa, who maintain favorable lipid profiles and low atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) incidence, despite a traditional diet high in lactose, saturated fat, and cholesterol [60,61]. Field studies have demonstrated reductions in serum cholesterol levels in response to increased dietary fat and cholesterol intake even in the context of rapid weight gain [62], and several polymorphisms in genes associated with both lactase persistence and cholesterol regulation have been identified in this population [63].

Conversely, it is also hypothesized that cultural reliance on fermented milk may have reduced the selective pressure for lactase persistence in some populations, such as the Central Asian pastoralists, instead promoting colonic adaptations to aid in lactose digestion [[64], [65], [66]]. In a 12-week single-blind trial among lactase-nonpersistent Asian adults, daily consumption of incremental lactose doses not only reduced intolerance symptoms but also demonstrated colonic adaptations, marked by enrichment of Bifidobacterium and β-galactosidase activity [65]. Such adaptations may concurrently influence inflammatory and metabolic pathways, potentially underlying epidemiological links between yogurt consumption and cardiometabolic health, as discussed in more detail in later sections.

Regardless of the pathway, the ability to consume dairy safely and access its nutritional benefits likely further reinforced herd expansion and more sophisticated animal husbandry, promoting broader adoption of dairying and its integration as a longstanding practice. Since its ancient origins, over 400 traditional and nontraditional fresh fermented milk products have now been documented, reflecting diverse microbial strains, milk sources, and fermentation techniques that give each product its distinct flavor, texture, and nutritional profile [67]. The cultural importance of fermented milk is reflected in the historical record. In the Book of Genesis, Abraham serves his visitors with “curds,” which is often interpreted as a form of sour or curdled milk akin to yogurt [68]. Similar references to dadhi (curd) appear in ancient Indian texts, where it is described as a milk product used in ritual, dietary, and medicinal contexts [69]. Moreover, writing in the 1 st century A.D., Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder remarked that “barbarous nations which subsist on milk … understand how to thicken milk and form there from an acrid kind of liquid with a pleasant flavor” [70].

The term yogurt derives from the Turkish verb yoğurmak, meaning “to thicken, coagulate, or curdle,” which was first documented in 11th-century Turkic texts [71]. It later entered the English language through Samuel Purchas’ travelogue in 1625, where he noted that the Turks preferred their milk soured, calling it “yoghurd” [72]. Further, historical accounts report that Mongol emperor Genghis Khan fed his army yogurt and kumis for health and bravery in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, and that yogurt was introduced to Western Europe in 1542 when Ottoman physicians reportedly treated King Francois I of France with fermented milk for severe diarrhea [73]. Despite early recognition of yogurt’s potential health benefits, scientific exploration did not commence until the early 20th century.

### Early scientific investigation of yogurt cultures

Yogurt is characterized by symbiotic cultures of Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus [74]. In 1904, Nobel laureate Élie Metchnikoff delivered a public lecture titled, “Old Age,” proposing that yogurt containing lactic acid bacteria could promote longevity by displacing putrefactive intestinal bacteria he believed precipitated aging, citing the unusually high percentage of centenarians in the Rhodope Mountains of southern Bulgaria, where yogurt was regularly consumed, as supportive evidence [75]. Metchnikoff’s presentation of his early hypothesis linking the gut to aging pathophysiology propelled yogurt into public consciousness as a health food and spurred scientific inquiry into its purported benefits.

Metchnikoff’s ideas gained early experimental support from Stamen Grigorov, who isolated L. bulgaricus from Bulgarian yogurt in 1905 [76], and Michel Cohendy, who conducted two human feeding trials in 1906 showing that L. bulgaricus was recoverable in feces, reduced putrefactive toxins, and aided in the treatment of colitis [77]. He expanded his hypothesis in The Prolongation of Life (1908), writing that manipulating the “wild population of the intestine into a cultured population… the pathological symptoms may be removed from old age, and… in all probability, the duration of the life of man may be considerably increased” [71]. Soon after, the Pasteur Institute began commercializing L. bulgaricus under the product name "Le Ferment” [77].

A significant challenge, however, emerged in the 1920s when Leo Rettger and colleagues at Yale University demonstrated that L. bulgaricus could not survive gastric passage to colonize the small intestine [78], raising questions about the organisms responsible for the therapeutic effects observed in earlier trials. Rettger proposed Lactobacillus acidophilus as a more viable candidate, given its ability to survive gastric passage and favorably alter intestinal flora [78,79], with early human studies reporting improvements in constipation, diarrhea, eczema, and mental disease following administration of this strain [80,81]. However, interest in L. acidophilus waned during World War II due to the urgent demand for penicillin production, only to resurge in the 1960s amid rising antibiotic resistance [82], leading to rapid expansion in probiotic research and commercialization over subsequent decades.

### Commercialization and spread of yogurt as a health food

In 1919, Isaac Carasso founded Danone in Spain (later rebranded to Dannon in North America), distributing yogurt through pharmacies as a medicinal product [76]. In the U.S., yogurt production began in 1929, when Armenian immigrants Sarkis Krikorian and Rose Colombosian launched Colombo & Sons Creamery in Andover, Massachusetts [83]. Initially regarded as an ethnic food and too tart for the American palate, yogurt’s appeal broadened with Danone’s introduction of fruit-on-the-bottom products in 1947. By the late 1970s and 1980s, low-fat yogurt products gained mainstream popularity, bolstered by Danone’s advertising campaigns claiming that “where they eat a lot of yogurt, a lot of people live past 100,” reinforcing its association with longevity [83]. This trend reflected prevailing nutrition evidence at the time, which implicated dietary fat, particularly saturated fat, in the rising prevalence of ASCVD and obesity, while downplaying the role of sugar [[84], [85], [86], [87]].

In the early 2000s, studies began linking added sugar with cardiometabolic disease [88,89], coinciding with the rise of Greek yogurt, which was largely niche until 2005, when Hamdi Ulukaya founded Chobani in upstate New York [90]. At the same time, growing consumer awareness of probiotics, driven in part by the proliferation of microbiome research in the 2000s and 2010s [91], repositioned yogurt not merely as a low-fat diet food but as a functional food with recognized health benefits. This shift corresponded to an eight-fold increase in biomedical yogurt research publications since the early 1970s [92], and a five-fold rise in U.S. yogurt consumption between 1981 and 2021, even as rates for fluid milk declined, cheese only doubled, and overall dairy grew only slightly [93]. More recently, in 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first qualified health claim for yogurt in 2024, permitting Danone to advertise that eating yogurt regularly may reduce the risk of T2D [94].

### Yogurt as a probiotic carrier and functional food

Beyond its starter cultures, yogurt is often a carrier of probiotic strains, most commonly from the Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium genera, which are primarily responsible for its functional properties [74,95,96]. Probiotics are defined as “live microorganisms, which when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host,” a definition established by the 2001 FAO/WHO expert consensus [95] and later refined by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) in 2014 [96].

Yogurt is an ideal carrier to deliver probiotics, as fermented dairy matrices more effectively protect bacteria from the harsh microbial environment during digestion compared with non-fermented dairy, capsules, or powder [97]. To qualify as a probiotic, yogurt products must contain sufficient doses of microorganisms that survive gastrointestinal transit, tolerate gastric acidity and bile, lack transferable antibiotic resistance genes, and demonstrate health benefits [74,95,96]. Although the 2002 FAO/WHO guidelines [98] recognized probiotic status for S. thermophilus and L. bulgaricus based on their documented ability to improve lactose digestion, standard yogurt is not considered a probiotic product as these starter cultures cannot proliferate in the gut. However, the classification of live microbes in fermented foods and the level of evidence required to substantiate health benefits remains debated.

## Modern scientific evidence linking yogurt and cardiometabolic health

Since its inception to now, the manufacturing and composition of commercial yogurt have continued to evolve throughout the world, where it has numerous different traditional names [99]. The compositional evolution of yogurt became especially pronounced following the development of industrial yogurt production processes in the late 1990s early 1920s [100]. Noticeable advancements include the addition of fruit to commercially available yogurt in the 1930s, with fruit on bottom becoming available in the 1940s, and blended products being developed in the 1960s [99]. Now, commercially available can be purchased with solid, semi-solid and fluid-like consistencies [101,102]. In many countries throughout the world, there is great variety in the nutritional composition of yogurt. In alignment with the Codex Alimentarius [74] and depending on local legislation and good manufacturing guidelines, yogurt products can differ widely in their concentration and characteristics of starter microorganisms, probiotic bacteria, yeast, fat, protein, sweeteners, water, gelatine, starch, stabilizers, thickeners, flavors, and acidity. Product formulation is often designed to achieve the specific organoleptic (sensory), nutritional, and health attributes their target consumers demand.

Despite the great product-specific variation in nutritional and health characteristics, in recent decades, observational studies have focused on testing the associations of total yogurt, and broad yogurt classes, have with important health outcomes such as cardiometabolic disease. Cardiometabolic disease is the leading contributor to age-related mortality and has important implications for healthy life expectancy [103,104]. Meta-analyses of cohort studies indicate that yogurt consumption is associated with lower CVD incidence and mortality [10,30]. In the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health study, substituting low-fat and whole milk for full-fat yogurt corresponded to an 11–13% lower risk of myocardial infarction (MI), whereas substitution for cheese yielded only a modest 4–5% reduction [105]. Similarly, data from the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (HPFS) show that higher yogurt intake was associated with a 17–21% lower risk of CVD (MI and stroke) among hypertensive men and women [106], and a 16% lower risk of incident hypertension among initially normotensive adults, while milk and cheese were associated with smaller reductions in hypertension risk (12% and 6%, respectively) [107]. Additional cohort studies further support this distinction, with yogurt intake associated with lower levels of inflammatory biomarkers such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and fibrin, as well as reduced common carotid artery intima-media thickness (CCA-IMT)—a surrogate marker for atherosclerosis—whereas neither milk nor cheese showed such associations [108,109].

Beyond CVD, meta-analyses consistently support an inverse relationship between yogurt consumption and T2D risk, while evidence for milk and cheese is generally more modest or null, though some studies suggest cheese may even be associated with higher risk [18,19,[31], [32], [33]]. For instance, a pooled analysis of the NHS I, NHS II, and HPFS cohorts found that increasing yogurt intake by >0.5 servings/day was associated with an 11% lower risk of T2D, whereas a comparable increase in cheese intake was linked to a 9% higher risk [33]. Notably, replacing one daily serving of cheese with yogurt or reduced-fat milk was linked to a 16% and 12% lower T2D risk, respectively [33]. Similarly, another meta-analysis reported that each 50-gram daily increase in yogurt intake was associated with a 7% lower risk of T2D and a 13% lower risk of overweight or obesity, whereas a larger 200-g increase in milk intake corresponded to a comparable reduction in overweight or obesity but not T2D [18].

Evidence also supports a protective role of yogurt against MetS. Meta-analyses report that total, low-fat, and full-fat yogurt intake are associated with 26%, 28%, and 19% lower MetS incidence, respectively, compared with a 21% reduction for total milk [34]. In the Prevención con Dieta Mediterránea (PREDIMED) study, participants in the highest tertiles of total, low-fat, and full-fat yogurt (23%, 27%, and 22%, respectively) and low-fat milk (20%) showed lower risk compared with the lowest tertiles, while total and whole milk showed no associations [110]. Conversely, cheese intake was linked to a 31% higher MetS risk in PREDIMED [110], a finding that conflicts with the inverse association reported in the Data from the Epidemiological Study on the Insulin Resistance Syndrome (DESIR) [111].

The PREDIMED study further showed that only full-fat yogurt was inversely associated with all five MetS components, including abdominal obesity, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and elevated triglycerides (TG), fasting blood glucose (FBG), and blood pressure (BP) [110]. Low-fat yogurt (HDL-C, TG, FBG) and low-fat milk (HDL-C, FBG) were associated with only a subset of components, and whole milk and cheese showed no associations [110]. Consistent with these findings, higher yogurt intake was linked to more favorable HDL-C and TG concentrations in the Million Veterans Program cohort, whereas milk and cheese showed no such associations [112]. Furthermore, yogurt interventions have demonstrated reductions in serum inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), with stronger reductions when probiotics are included [[113], [114], [115], [116], [117], [118], [119]]. In a meta-analysis, probiotic yogurt was also shown to reduce total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [120].

Despite the capacity for the tremendous inter-product variance in its nutritional and health characteristics, observational studies of commercially available yogurt generally report beneficial associations with cardiometabolic health and outcomes. One possible explanation is the core compositional elements laid out in the Codex Alimentarius [74], which are shared across most yogurt products. However, the contribution of product-specific differences in formulation to the variance in the health benefits of yogurt are yet to be fully elucidated.

### Potential mechanisms

Modern research provides mechanistic support to Metchnikoff’s century-old hypothesis linking yogurt to the gut microbiome and healthy aging. It is now recognized that aging is accompanied by progressive shifts in the gut microbiome, including reduced microbial diversity, loss of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, and increased colonization of pro-inflammatory species, which collectively promote chronic low-grade inflammation and metabolic dysfunction [3,121]. Yogurt introduces live cultures that may help restore microbial balance and favorably modulate these pathways. Probiotics also undergo adaptive mechanisms in vivo through their interactions with the gut microbiota, which modify their capacity to generate bioactive compounds relevant to host health [97,122,123]. These include SCFAs, bioactive peptides, and exopolysaccharides, all of which may attenuate some of the potential negative effects of saturated fat on cardiometabolic health [28,29].

Regular yogurt consumption is associated with a distinct gut microbiome and metabolome, including enrichment of resident taxa such as Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Christensenellaceae, as well as yogurt-derived Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, and Bifidobacterium species [4,5]. Many of these taxa have been proposed as microbial signatures associated with healthy aging, as they are more abundant in centenarians compared with young adults [[124], [125], [126], [127], [128], [129], [130]]. Age-related microbial shifts also alter the production of gut microbiota-derived metabolites capable of influencing host metabolism and inflammation, including SCFAs, secondary bile acids (SBAs), and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) [1], which may explain some of yogurt’s unique influence on reducing risk of adverse age-related health outcomes.

### Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)

SCFAs, including acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are primarily generated by colonic fermentation of dietary fibers and resistant starch, and to a lesser extent, peptides and amino acids that escape small intestinal absorption [131]. Smaller amounts are also present in yogurt and other fermented foods [132]. Aging is associated with reduced SCFA production, which can compromise gut barrier integrity, allow microbial translocation into the bloodstream, and promote systemic inflammation [133,134]. Thus, yogurt's anti-inflammatory effects are likely mediated, in part, through its modulation of SCFA-producing bacteria.

Yogurt consumption has been associated with enrichment of butyrate-producing bacteria [4,5] and increased fecal butyrate concentrations [135]. As the most clinically relevant SCFA, butyrate serves as the primary energy source for colonocytes, maintains intestinal barrier integrity, and modulates immune function and inflammatory responses [136,137]. Butyrate is largely produced by resident taxa within Lachnospiraceae (e.g., Eubacterium, Roseburia, Anaerostripes) and Ruminococcaceae (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) [138], while certain Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species contribute by generating acetate and lactate that can be further cross-fed to butyrate-producing bacteria [139]. Yogurt fortified with prebiotic fibers has also been shown to improve body composition and metabolic profiles, as prebiotic fibers provide additional fermentable substrate for SCFA-producing bacteria, potentially amplifying these effects [140,141].

### Secondary bile acids (SBAs)

Bile acids facilitate lipid digestion and absorption and act as signaling molecules that regulate their own metabolism, as well as key aspects of lipid, glucose, and energy homeostasis and systemic inflammation [142]. Primary bile acids (PBAs) are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver and secreted into the intestines, where certain resident bacteria deconjugate and in some cases, dehydroxylate them to form SBAs. Most bile acids are reabsorbed and recycled into enterohepatic circulation, while a small fraction is excreted in the feces [143]. However, gut dysbiosis can reduce bile acid excretion and promote pathologic accumulation of circulatory SBAs, contributing to metabolic dysfunction, systemic inflammation, and increased cardiometabolic risk [144,145].

Yogurt consumption may help maintain a balanced bile acid pool by modulating microbial communities to prevent the overgrowth of SBA-producing bacteria, which may reduce systemic inflammation by shifting balance of the pro-inflammatory SBAs toward anti-inflammatory SCFAs [146]. Specific probiotic strains in yogurt, primarily Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium [5], encode bile salt hydrolase (BSH) enzymes that deconjugate PBAs, reducing their reabsorption [147]. Moreover, calcium and exopolysaccharides (EPS) naturally present in yogurt, along with prebiotic fibers often added to commercial formulations, can bind free bile acids in the intestines [148,149]. These mechanisms increase fecal bile acid excretion, which stimulates hepatic synthesis of PBAs from cholesterol, thereby lowering circulating cholesterol levels [120].

### Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO)

TMAO is considered an independent and dose-dependent risk factor for cardiovascular risk [[150], [151], [152]], with elevated levels associated with greater CCA-IMT [152] and increased risk of CVD, T2D, obesity, hypertension, and MetS [[153], [154], [155], [156], [157]]. It is produced by gut microbial metabolism of nutrients such as choline, lecithin, betaine, and l-carnitine, which are abundant in dairy products, egg yolks, red meat, and saltwater fish [158]. Certain gut bacteria metabolize these nutrients into trimethylamine (TMA), which is then converted into TMAO in the liver. Overgrowth of TMA-producing bacteria can therefore increase TMAO production to pathological levels, which disrupts cholesterol metabolism and promotes vascular inflammation [157,159], although it has also been proposed that TMAO might function as an adaptive, protective mechanism within a certain concentration range [160]. This may partly explain why fish intake, despite being a significant source of TMAO [161,162], is associated with lower atherosclerotic risk [163], and why some animal studies suggest TMAO may have neutral or beneficial effects on cardiometabolic health [164,165].

Although dairy contains TMAO precursors, fermented products such as yogurt may lower systemic TMAO production by modulating the gut microbiota, particularly when probiotics are included. For example, a crossover RCT showed that yogurt containing L. rhamnosus GG was associated with reduced plasma and urinary TMAO levels postprandially compared with acidified milk, whereas cheese only reduced urinary concentrations relative to milk [166]. A recent systematic review further suggests that L. rhamnosus GG may be the most effective probiotic strain in reducing plasma TMAO concentrations in humans [167]. Additional strains, including L. plantarum ZDY04 and Enterococcus faecium WEFA23, have also been shown to lower plasma TMAO, reduce serum cholesterol, and inhibit the development of atherosclerosis in animal studies [168,169].

## Current limitations and future directions

Despite promising associations linking yogurt consumption to favorable cardiometabolic outcomes, current evidence is limited by several factors. Most studies are observational, making it difficult to establish causality and leaving results susceptible to confounding by overall diet, lifestyle, or socioeconomic factors. Long-term aging-focused randomized controlled trials are relatively few and typically focus on surrogate endpoints rather than long-term clinical outcomes. Moreover, the effects of yogurt on the gut microbiome and its downstream mechanisms remain poorly characterized, and evidence from long-term, population-based follow-up is scarce. These gaps highlight the need for more rigorous, mechanistic, and longitudinal research in aging-specific cohorts to clarify yogurt’s therapeutic potential.

Furthermore, yogurt products themselves are heterogeneous in fat and protein content, added sugars, and live cultures, complicating comparisons across studies. This is particularly relevant given the increasing availability and consumption of yogurt products containing added sugars, flavorings, colorings, stabilizers, and other ingredients that may substantially alter their nutritional profiles compared with plain, minimally processed yogurt. Whether these products confer similar health benefits remains uncertain. To that end, although evidence specifically evaluating high-protein yogurt is still limited, intervention studies suggest that plain Greek or other minimally processed high-protein yogurts retain the beneficial characteristics of conventional yogurt while providing additional protein that may enhance satiety [170,171]. However, prospective cohort studies evaluating cardiometabolic outcomes assess total yogurt intake using food frequency questionnaires or dietary recalls and do not consistently distinguish between plain, high-protein, flavored, sweetened, or more highly processed yogurt products. Consequently, potential exposure misclassification may attenuate or obscure associations between specific yogurt subtypes and health outcomes. Therefore, future epidemiological studies should differentiate yogurt subtypes according to both protein content and degree of processing.

With ongoing advances in precision fermentation and multi-omics (e.g., metagenomics, metabolomics, host genomics), there is an opportunity to develop personalized microgenomic medicine based on an individual’s phenotype. Realizing this potential will require integrating host-microbe interplay by leveraging baseline microbiota profiling (including enterotype classification and α-diversity) to identify likely responders to specific fermented formulations, incorporating host genomic data to capture variation in mucosal glycosylation and immune function that shapes microbial engraftment and metabolism, and applying machine learning to multi-omics datasets to iteratively refine strain selection, dosing, and food matrix composition over time [28]. By integrating these components, precision fermentation can shift from broad, population-level guidance to tailored approaches that enhance gut microbiome modulation and improve clinical outcomes for each individual.

## Conclusions

From its ancient origins to modern scientific inquiry, yogurt has evolved into a compelling model for understanding host-microbe interactions. Although Metchnikoff’s original theory of longevity was tempered over time into more modest expectations of treating digestive complaints, contemporary research has begun to substantiate yogurt’s potential applications beyond the gut. While findings should not necessarily be generalized to all fermented dairy products, yogurt is now among the most extensively studied foods, with growing evidence suggesting potential benefits for cardiometabolic, neurological, skeletal, and immune health. This has ultimately transformed yogurt from a general health food into a functional food that may promote healthy aging trajectories, resilience, and preservation of metabolic and immune function with aging, thus extending Metchnikoff’s foundational vision as a vehicle for longevity. Advances in precision fermentation and multi-omics further point toward a future in which probiotic strains could be tailored to individual host genetics, gut microbiome composition, and metabolic profiles, positioning yogurt into a potential bioprophylactic or biotherapeutic tool. While our understanding of the vast microbiome is likely still in its infancy, if yogurt consumption can indeed help prevent or manage age-related diseases and improve health and well-being among aging populations, then perhaps it can “prolong life.”
